We hold a remembered account of how Ephrem spent his last year:
In the last year of Ephrem's life, famine struck Edessa.
Palladius of Galatia and Sozomen, a Greek historian, both tell of that year, writing a generation and more after his death.
Their count of beds and the words they report come from remembered tradition.
For many years Ephrem had lived quietly in his cell, but now he left it and went to the rich of the city.
He asked them why they had no pity on people dying around them, while their wealth spoiled into the condemnation of their own souls.
The rich answered that they had no one they could trust with the giving, because everyone was dishonest in such business.
Ephrem asked what they thought of him, and they said they knew him to be a man of God.
"Then trust me," he said.
"See, on your behalf I appoint myself to take in and care for the needy."
He took their money and set up some three hundred beds in the public porches.
There he nursed the starving and the sick, strangers and local people alike, and he buried those who died.
When the year was over and good times returned, he went back to his cell.
He died soon after, a month later in Palladius's account and a few days later in Sozomen's.

Our city chronicle keeps one early trace of us:
In November of the year 513 of the Greeks, around the year 201, the river Daisan rose against Edessa in the night.
King Abgar stood on the great tower and watched the water by torchlight.
That same hour the waters broke down the western wall and swept through the city, overthrowing the king's palace.
The Chronicle of Edessa sets down this account.
It was compiled about 340 years later from the archives where the royal scribes had filed it.
No bishop or believer is named in it.
One line among the losses matters most to us.
"And they destroyed the temple of the church of the Christians."
Whether the line is original, or was added later by another hand, is not settled.
If it is original, a church building stood in Edessa to be destroyed, and that line is our earliest hard trace.
"More than two thousand men were killed in that event. The waters came upon many of them suddenly as they slept in the night, and they drowned. The city was filled with the sound of mourning."

rewrite.sentence: We would have met you as someone still raising a house, because faith among us was a building that goes up piece by piece.
What we distrusted was not the struggling believer.
What we distrusted was the prying scrutinizer, who would take the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved.
Aphrahat gave an order, not a short list.
First a man believes, and when he believes, he loves.
When a man loves, he hopes; when he hopes, he is justified, and then he is made perfect.
Fasting, prayer, alms and meekness are built on faith.
For the one who falls, Aphrahat named penitence as the medicine for the wound.
We name no single act that secures life, and we pass no verdict on you, for Aphrahat leaves the reckoning to the judge.

rewrite.sentence: Our certainties were these: death is beaten, judgment is real and just, and the door stands open while life lasts.
We drew far less of the modern map of who exactly burns than people assume.
Our confidence lay in the Judge, not in a roster.
The Kingdom repays everyone what is due and admits the invited with distinction, and we sang the warning as urgently as the hope.
The dialogue from Bardaisan's school said that Christ, at his coming, planted one new people in every country.
Our sage Aphrahat wrote that every man will receive his reward by his work, and that the judge will rebuke those with a small fault and then give them the inheritance of life.
Our argument against Jewish practice was real, and only our side of it was kept.
Roughly four of our sage's letters argue against the Jews with a bitterness the record never balances.
